sessions.title: Linear maps preserve combinations
sessions.focus: Define finite real linear maps before matrices, test superposition, and use basis images to determine the whole map.
sessions.purpose: Make the object primary: a matrix will later represent a linear map, so the learner first needs a precise map-level contract independent of any array arithmetic.
sessions.centralCapability: Verify or refute linearity from the defining laws and compute a linear map on arbitrary vectors from its action on a basis.
sessions.principalObstacle: A simple-looking or line-preserving rule is accepted as linear without testing superposition, while a basis-action specification is mistaken for incomplete information.
entryPrerequisites: M13 finite real vectors and linear combinations
requiredOwnership: Verify linearity by preservation of vector addition and scalar multiplication, equivalently finite linear combinations.
Derive and use T(0)=0 as a necessary consequence of linearity.
Explain why a linear map is uniquely determined by its values on a basis.
Compute the action of a linear map on an arbitrary vector from basis images.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite-dimensional real coordinate spaces and exact algebra; affine translations may appear only as counterexamples.
sessions.transferScope: Transfer removes the coordinate formula for one map and gives only basis action, while contrasting it with an affine-looking formula.
sessions.exitCondition: Given a formula or basis-action description, determine whether a rule is linear and, when linear, determine its action on arbitrary vectors.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. A transformation is a rule T:V→W taking vectors in a domain V to vectors in a codomain W. Before arrays of numbers enter, the structural question is whether T respects the operations M13 already owns. T is linear when T(u+v)=T(u)+T(v) for every u,v in V and T(cu)=cT(u) for every real c. Combining the two gives T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v), and repeating gives preservation of every finite linear combination.

A forced consequence is T(0)=0. Since 0=0+0, linearity gives T(0)=T(0)+T(0), hence T(0)=0 after subtracting T(0). Therefore a nonzero translation can be rejected immediately, but passing the zero test alone does not prove linearity.

Basis bridge. If B=(b1,...,bn) is a basis and v=x1b1+...+xnbn, uniqueness of M13 coordinates gives T(v)=x1T(b1)+...+xnT(bn). So once a linear map's images of the basis vectors are known, every output is forced; two linear maps that agree on a basis agree everywhere.

Worked example. Let T:R²→R² satisfy T(x,y)=(2x-y,x+3y). For arbitrary scalars a,b and vectors u=(u1,u2), v=(v1,v2), expanding each coordinate gives T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v), so the rule is linear. With e1=(1,0), e2=(0,1), T(e1)=(2,1) and T(e2)=(-1,3). Thus T(3,-2)=3T(e1)-2T(e2)=(8,-3).

Guided practice. Compare G(x,y)=(x-y,2y) with H(x,y)=(x-y+2,2y). Before checking, test the zero vector and decide which rule is immediately disqualified. For the surviving rule, compute the images of e1,e2 and reconstruct the output at (2,-1) using only those images.

Distinction check. “Straight-looking formula” and “linear transformation” are not synonyms. An affine translation may preserve lines geometrically while failing T(0)=0 and superposition. Conversely, a map can be specified completely by basis images without an explicit coordinate formula.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. H(0,0)=(2,0), so H cannot be linear. G(e1)=(1,0) and G(e2)=(-1,2); therefore G(2,-1)=2G(e1)-G(e2)=(3,-2).

sessions.title: A matrix is a map written in chosen coordinates
sessions.focus: Construct the matrix of a linear map from transformed basis vectors and track input/output basis order and shape.
sessions.purpose: Turn S01's basis-action theorem into a coordinate representation without letting the representation replace the underlying map.
sessions.centralCapability: Given ordered domain and codomain bases, construct or decode the matrix representing a linear map and explain its dimensions and column meanings.
sessions.principalObstacle: Columns are treated as arbitrary coefficient lists, basis order is ignored, or the matrix is mistaken for the underlying map independent of coordinate choices.
entryPrerequisites: M14-S01 linear maps and basis action
M13 ordered bases and unique coordinates
requiredOwnership: Construct a matrix representation by placing the codomain-coordinate vectors of transformed domain-basis vectors as columns.
Infer and justify the m-by-n shape from an n-dimensional domain basis and m-dimensional codomain basis, with basis order respected.
Recover transformed basis vectors from matrix columns and distinguish the represented map from its basis-dependent matrix.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite real spaces with explicitly named ordered bases; standard-basis cases are special cases.
sessions.transferScope: Transfer begins with a matrix and basis labels rather than a transformation rule and asks the learner to recover the map's basis action.
sessions.exitCondition: Move reliably between basis-action data and a correctly typed matrix representation.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. S01 showed that a linear map is completely determined by what it does to a basis. A matrix packages exactly that finite information. Let B=(b1,...,bn) be an ordered basis of V and C=(c1,...,cm) an ordered basis of W. The matrix A=[T]_{C←B} is the m-by-n array whose jth column is the C-coordinate vector [T(bj)]_C.

Why columns? If [v]_B=(x1,...,xn)^T, then v=Σ xj bj and linearity gives T(v)=Σ xj T(bj). Taking C-coordinates therefore gives [T(v)]_C=x1[T(b1)]_C+...+xn[T(bn)]_C. The coordinate vectors of the basis images must be the columns because the input coordinates are their combination weights.

Worked example. Let B=(b1,b2,b3) and C=(c1,c2). Suppose T(b1)=c1+2c2, T(b2)=-2c1+c2 and T(b3)=3c2. Then [T]_{C←B} has columns (1,2)^T, (-2,1)^T, (0,3)^T, so A=[[1,-2,0],[2,1,3]]. For v=2b1-b2+b3, [v]_B=(2,-1,1)^T and the same column combination gives [T(v)]_C=(4,6)^T. This calculation follows from the map; the array did not create the rule.

Guided practice. A map S has ordered input basis D=(d1,d2) and output basis E=(e1,e2,e3), with S(d1)=2e1-e3 and S(d2)=e2+4e3. Before checking, build [S]_{E←D}, state its shape, and say what the second column means.

Distinction check. T is the coordinate-free rule; [T]_{C←B} is one representation after bases are named. Changing a basis can change the entries even though the underlying map has not changed. S17–S18 will develop the conversion machinery.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. The columns are [S(d1)]_E=(2,0,-1)^T and [S(d2)]_E=(0,1,4)^T, so [S]_{E←D}=[[2,0],[0,1],[-1,4]], a 3-by-2 matrix. The second column is the E-coordinate vector of S(d2).

sessions.title: Matrix-vector action is a column combination
sessions.focus: Interpret Ax simultaneously as a weighted combination of matrix columns and as row dot-products, with dimensions fixed before arithmetic.
sessions.purpose: Make matrix-vector multiplication a meaningful coordinate action rather than a memorized row-by-column ritual.
sessions.centralCapability: Compute and interpret Ax from column structure, reconcile the row and column views, and use basis-vector probes to recover a represented map.
sessions.principalObstacle: The learner can execute row-dot arithmetic while losing the input/output meaning, confusing rows with columns, or accepting dimensionally illegal products.
entryPrerequisites: M13 vector combinations and dot products
requiredOwnership: Compute Ax as the linear combination of A's columns weighted by the coordinates of x.
Reconcile the column-combination and row-dot-product calculations as two views of the same output.
Use matrix shape and basis-vector probes Ae_j to infer legal input/output dimensions and recover column responses.
sessions.applicationScope: Exact finite matrices and coordinate vectors; no numerical storage/performance issues.
sessions.transferScope: Transfer presents unit-input response data from a model and asks the learner to assemble the matrix and predict a mixed input.
sessions.exitCondition: Given a matrix and vector or unit-response table, compute the output and explain what the dimensions and columns mean.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. An m-by-n matrix A has n columns a1,...,an, each in R^m. An input x=(x1,...,xn)^T supplies the weights for one linear combination: Ax=x1a1+...+xnan. This is exactly S02's basis-action theorem written in coordinates. Therefore A accepts n-coordinate inputs and produces m-coordinate outputs.

Rows give the same numbers from another view. The ith component of Ax is ai1x1+...+ainxn, the dot product of row i with x. Column combination explains *what output is being assembled*; row dots explain how each output coordinate is calculated. They are not competing definitions.

Basis probes. If ej is the jth standard basis vector of R^n, then Aej=aj because all weights except xj are zero. So testing a black-box linear map on the standard basis recovers every column of its standard matrix.

Worked example. Let A=[[1,-2],[3,0],[-1,4]] and x=(2,-1)^T. With columns a1=(1,3,-1)^T and a2=(-2,0,4)^T, Ax=2a1-a2=(4,6,-6)^T. Row dots give 1·2+(-2)(-1)=4, 3·2=6, and -1·2+4(-1)=-6. The 3-by-2 shape predicts an R² input and R³ output before calculating.

Guided practice. For B=[[2,0,-1],[1,3,2]] and x=(1,-1,2)^T, compute Bx first as a combination of its three columns, then check both output coordinates with row dots. State the legal input and output dimensions.

Distinction check. “Multiply the row by the column” is a useful computation, but it hides the map structure if taught alone. A matrix-vector product is not entrywise multiplication, and a dimension mismatch is a type error rather than a difficult arithmetic case.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. B is 2-by-3, so x∈R^3 and Bx∈R^2. Columnwise, Bx=(2,1)-(0,3)+2(-1,2)=(0,2). Row dots give 2+0-2=0 and 1-3+4=2.

sessions.title: Composition makes matrix multiplication inevitable
sessions.focus: Derive matrix multiplication from composition of represented linear maps, including order, dimensions, product columns and noncommutativity.
sessions.purpose: Give the matrix-matrix product a structural reason before any rote multiplication routine can harden into the learner's mental model.
sessions.centralCapability: For a chain of compatible linear maps, choose the correct product order, compute the composite matrix, and interpret what the product's columns and dimensions mean.
sessions.principalObstacle: A learner may compute row-by-column correctly while reversing process order, treating multiplication as commutative, or checking only that dimensions happen to allow a product.
entryPrerequisites: M14-S01 linear maps and composition language
requiredOwnership: Translate a stated composition of linear maps into the correct ordered matrix product with compatible intermediate dimensions.
Compute a matrix product and interpret each product column as the outer map applied to the corresponding inner-map column.
Explain why matrix multiplication is associative through associativity of map composition when dimensions are compatible.
Reject commutativity in general using a concrete pair for which both products are legal but represent different process orders.
sessions.applicationScope: Exact finite matrices with explicitly tracked source, intermediate and target coordinate spaces.
sessions.transferScope: Transfer changes from abstract map symbols and a rectangular chain to a verbal two-stage square processing pipeline where both multiplication orders are legal.
sessions.exitCondition: Given unfamiliar maps or a verbal linear pipeline, construct and defend the correct composite matrix rather than relying on an order mnemonic.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. Suppose T:U→V is represented by B and S:V→W is represented by A in compatible chosen bases. For an input coordinate vector x, T produces Bx and then S produces A(Bx). The composite S∘T therefore satisfies [S∘T]x=A(Bx)=(AB)x. This defines the useful product order: the map applied first appears on the right.

Dimensions follow the spaces, not a memorized slogan. If B is n-by-p and A is m-by-n, then B maps p coordinates to n coordinates and A maps n to m; AB is m-by-p. The shared n is the intermediate coordinate dimension. The jth column of AB is A times the jth column of B, because that column is what the inner map does to the jth input basis vector.

Worked example. Let B=[[2,0],[1,1]] and A=[[1,1],[0,2]]. Then AB=[[3,1],[2,2]], representing “B first, then A.” Reversing the process gives BA=[[2,2],[1,3]], which is also legal but different. Thus AB≠BA in general. Multiplication is nevertheless associative when shapes permit: three compatible maps R,S,T have only one composed map R∘S∘T, so ([R][S])[T]=[R]([S][T]).

Guided practice. Let D=[[1,2],[0,1],[-1,1]] represent T:R²→R³ and C=[[1,0,1],[2,-1,0]] represent S:R³→R². Before checking, decide the shape of the matrix for S∘T, compute CD by treating its columns as C times the columns of D, and interpret its first column as a composed basis response.

Distinction check. Dimension compatibility is necessary but not enough to determine which process a product represents. When both AB and BA are legal, semantic order decides. Matrix multiplication is composition in coordinates, not entrywise multiplication and not a commutative arithmetic inherited from scalars.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. D maps R^2→R^3 and C maps R^3→R^2, so S∘T has matrix CD of shape 2-by-2. CD=[[0,3],[2,3]]. Its first column (0,2)^T is C applied to D's first column (1,0,-1)^T, i.e. the output of S(T(e1)).

sessions.title: A linear system has row and column meanings
sessions.focus: Translate simultaneous scalar equations into Ax=b and interpret the same statement as intersecting row constraints and as a column-combination reachability question.
sessions.purpose: Make the system's solution set and the meaning of Ax=b explicit before an elimination algorithm changes its representation.
sessions.centralCapability: Formulate a finite linear system as Ax=b, move between row and column views, and use a coefficient witness or obstruction to interpret exact solvability.
sessions.principalObstacle: The equation array is treated as notation only; learners may forget that a solution must satisfy every row simultaneously or that the unknown coordinates are weights on A's columns.
requiredOwnership: Translate a finite system of scalar linear equations into a correctly typed matrix equation Ax=b.
Interpret the row view as simultaneous scalar constraints and the column view as a linear combination of A's columns equaling b.
Use a coefficient witness or contradiction to decide exact solvability in an elementary system without relying on equation-count heuristics.
sessions.applicationScope: Exact finite systems; geometric row pictures are used only where dimensions make them meaningful.
sessions.transferScope: Transfer changes from a written system to a response-library reachability problem whose unit responses are the columns.
sessions.exitCondition: Given equations or a column-response model, formulate Ax=b and explain what a solution means in both representations.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. A system of linear equations asks for one unknown vector x that satisfies several scalar constraints at once. Writing the coefficient rows into a matrix A and the constants into a vector b gives Ax=b. This is not new mathematics pasted into a compact notation: S03 tells us exactly what the statement means from two complementary views.

Row view. If row i of A is ri, then the ith equation is ri·x=bi. A solution must lie on every row constraint simultaneously. In two or three unknowns those constraints may be drawn as lines or planes, but the algebraic statement remains valid in any finite dimension.

Column view. If A=[a1 ... an] and x=(x1,...,xn)^T, then Ax=x1a1+...+xnan. Solving Ax=b therefore asks whether the target b can be assembled from the columns with coefficients xj. This reconnects M14 systems to M13 span membership without yet naming the full column-space object.

Worked example. Let A have columns a1=(1,0,2), a2=(2,-1,1), a3=(0,1,1), and let b=(5,-3,3). The vector x=(1,2,-1) gives a1+2a2-a3=(5,-3,3), so it is a solution. Written by rows, the same witness satisfies x1+2x2=5, -x2+x3=-3, and 2x1+x2+x3=3. One vector has satisfied all three constraints.

Guided practice. Convert the system 2u-v=1, u+3v=7 into Ax=b. Then rewrite Ax as a combination of A's two columns and verify that (u,v)=(2,3) is *not* a solution before finding the actual pair by elementary scalar algebra.

Distinction check. Three equations in three unknowns do not guarantee one solution. Dependence or inconsistency can produce many or no solutions. S06–S07 will expose that structure systematically instead of counting equations.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. A=[[2,-1],[1,3]], x=(u,v)^T and b=(1,7)^T. Ax=u(2,1)^T+v(-1,3)^T. At (2,3), the first component is 1 but the second is 11, so it is not a solution. Solving gives v=13/7 and u=10/7.

sessions.title: Row operations preserve the solution set
sessions.focus: Encode a system as an augmented matrix and justify elementary row operations as reversible transformations of the same simultaneous constraints.
sessions.purpose: Establish why elimination is legal before asking the learner to trust a row-reduction procedure.
sessions.centralCapability: Apply elementary row operations to an augmented system and prove that each legal step preserves exactly the same solutions.
sessions.principalObstacle: Rows are manipulated as detached number strings, the right-hand side is forgotten, or an irreversible operation such as multiplying a row by zero is treated as harmless.
requiredOwnership: Represent Ax=b as an augmented matrix [A|b] and apply a row operation to every entry of the affected equation, including b.
Justify row swap, nonzero row scaling and row replacement as reversible operations that preserve the exact solution set.
Diagnose an invalid or incompletely applied row operation and explain how it can change the represented system.
sessions.applicationScope: Exact finite systems; row operations are equation transformations, not numerical pivoting strategy.
sessions.transferScope: Transfer audits a proposed elimination step that changes coefficients but not the augmented constant and asks for a corrected operation.
sessions.exitCondition: Carry out and justify legal row operations while preserving the represented solution set exactly.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. Row operations are legal because each row stands for an equation, and the allowed moves replace a system by an *equivalent* system with exactly the same solutions. Write Ax=b as the augmented matrix [A|b] so the constants travel with their equations.

There are three elementary moves. (1) Swap two rows: reordering simultaneous equations changes no solution. (2) Multiply a row by a nonzero scalar c: multiplying both sides of an equation by c is reversible by multiplying by 1/c. (3) Replace Ri by Ri+cRj for i≠j: any old solution satisfies the new equation; conversely subtracting cRj recovers the old Ri. Reversibility is the key. Multiplying a row by zero is not reversible and can erase a constraint.

Worked example. From 2x+y=5 and 4x+3y=11, [A|b]=[[2,1|5],[4,3|11]]. Replace R2 by R2-2R1 to get [[2,1|5],[0,1|1]]. The constant 11 becomes 1 along with the coefficients. Every old solution satisfies the new second equation because it is equation 2 minus twice equation 1, and adding twice row 1 reverses the step.

Guided practice. For [[1,2,-1|3],[2,5,1|8],[-1,0,2|1]], perform R2←R2-2R1 and R3←R3+R1. Write the whole resulting augmented matrix and name the inverse operation for each step.

Distinction check. Row reduction changes the *representation* of the system, not its solution set. It can and usually does change the literal rows and columns of A, which will matter when S10 discusses column space.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. The two replacements give [[1,2,-1|3],[0,1,3|2],[0,2,1|4]]. The inverse steps are R2←R2+2R1 and R3←R3-R1. Each constant changed with its row.

sessions.title: Pivots and free variables classify exact solutions
sessions.focus: Reduce exact systems to echelon form, identify pivot/free variables, and distinguish inconsistent, unique and underdetermined cases.
sessions.purpose: Turn legal row operations into structural information about the entire solution set rather than just a way to obtain one numerical answer.
sessions.centralCapability: Use echelon structure to classify a finite exact system and parameterize every solution when free variables remain.
sessions.principalObstacle: The learner counts equations versus unknowns, treats a zero row as automatically inconsistent, or reports one particular vector when infinitely many solutions exist.
requiredOwnership: Reduce a small exact system to row-echelon form while tracking pivots and free variables.
Classify a system as inconsistent, uniquely solvable or infinitely solvable from contradiction rows and pivot/free-variable structure.
Parameterize all solutions of a consistent underdetermined system and verify the parameterized family.
sessions.applicationScope: Exact finite systems; RREF may be used when helpful but is not required if echelon/back-substitution suffices.
sessions.transferScope: Transfer keeps the coefficient pattern but changes the right-hand side so a previously redundant row becomes a contradiction.
sessions.exitCondition: Read an echelon system structurally and report the complete exact solution set, not merely a sample solution.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. Elimination has a destination: an echelon system where leading nonzero entries, or pivots, step to the right as we move down. Variables whose columns contain pivots are pivot variables; the remaining variables are free. The pattern tells us how many choices survive after all constraints are enforced.

Three cases. A row [0 ... 0|c] with c≠0 says 0=c and makes the system inconsistent. If no contradiction occurs and every variable column has a pivot, back-substitution gives one unique solution. If no contradiction occurs but at least one variable is free, each free choice generates a solution family, so there are infinitely many real solutions.

Worked example. For x+y+z=4, 2x+3y+z=7 and x+2y=3, use R2←R2-2R1 and R3←R3-R1. The last two rows both become y-z=-1, so one is redundant. With z=t free, y=t-1 and x=5-2t. Thus every solution is (5-2t,t-1,t), t∈R. Substitution into all three original equations verifies the family.

Guided practice. Reduce x+y+z=2, 2x+2y+2z=4, and y-z=1. Identify pivot and free variables, choose a parameter, and write every solution. Then imagine only the second right-hand side changes from 4 to 5; predict the contradiction before checking.

Distinction check. A zero row [0 ... 0|0] removes no solutions; it records a redundant equation. A contradiction row [0 ... 0|c], c≠0, destroys all solutions. Equation count alone does not distinguish them.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. Row 2 is twice row 1, so it reduces to [0,0,0|0]. With y-z=1, let z=t, then y=1+t and x=1-2t; every solution is (1-2t,1+t,t). If the second right-hand side were 5, subtracting 2R1 would instead give [0,0,0|1], so there would be no solution.

sessions.title: The null space records inputs erased by a map
sessions.focus: Define N(A)={x:Ax=0}, prove it is a subspace, and construct a basis from homogeneous free-variable solutions.
sessions.purpose: Promote homogeneous-solution mechanics into a reusable domain-side object that will control ambiguity, rank-nullity and invertibility.
sessions.centralCapability: Compute and interpret a null-space basis while keeping the null space in the input/domain space.
sessions.principalObstacle: The null space is confused with a set of output vectors, the zero right-hand side is thought to force only x=0, or special solutions are listed without proving they span every homogeneous solution.
requiredOwnership: Prove that N(A)={x:Ax=0} is a subspace of the domain by closure under linear combinations.
Solve Ax=0 and construct a basis for N(A) from independent free-variable special solutions.
Interpret a nonzero null vector as an input direction erased by the represented linear map and identify the correct ambient domain.
sessions.applicationScope: Exact finite real matrices; nullspace and kernel are treated as the same domain-side object.
sessions.transferScope: Transfer changes to a four-parameter response map and asks for two invisible parameter directions rather than a textbook homogeneous-system presentation.
sessions.exitCondition: Given a matrix, compute and explain its null space as the full set of invisible input directions.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. The homogeneous equation Ax=0 asks which inputs the map erases completely. Its solution set is the null space (or kernel) N(A). Because x is an input to A, N(A) lives in the domain R^n for an m-by-n matrix, not in the output R^m.

Subspace proof. Zero is in N(A) because A0=0. If u,v∈N(A) and a,b are real, then A(au+bv)=aAu+bAv=0, so every linear combination stays in N(A). This is a direct use of S01 linearity and proves N(A) is a subspace.

Worked example. For A=[[1,2,-1],[2,4,-2]], Ax=0 reduces to x1+2x2-x3=0. Let x2=s and x3=t. Then x1=-2s+t, so x=s(-2,1,0)+t(1,0,1). The two displayed special solutions are independent and every null vector is their combination, hence they form a basis. Each is a nonzero input that produces zero output.

Guided practice. For B=[[1,0,1,2],[0,1,-1,1]], solve Bx=0 with x3=s,x4=t. Construct the two special solutions and state the ambient space of N(B).

Distinction check. The zero right-hand side guarantees that x=0 is one solution; it does not guarantee uniqueness. A nontrivial null space means different inputs can have the same output, a fact S09 will make explicit.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. The equations give x1=-x3-2x4 and x2=x3-x4. Thus x=s(-1,1,1,0)+t(-2,-1,0,1). These two independent vectors span N(B), which is a subspace of the input space R^4.

sessions.title: Every consistent solution set is a translated null space
sessions.focus: Derive the complete solution of Ax=b as one particular solution plus N(A), and distinguish affine solution sets from subspaces.
sessions.purpose: Connect consistency and ambiguity: once one input reaches b, every other input reaching b differs by an invisible null direction.
sessions.centralCapability: Construct and prove the full affine solution set xp+N(A) for a consistent nonhomogeneous system.
sessions.principalObstacle: The learner reports a single particular solution as 'the solution', or incorrectly calls a translated solution set a subspace because it is parallel to one.
requiredOwnership: Prove that if Axp=b then every solution of Ax=b is exactly xp+n with n∈N(A).
Construct a complete parameterized solution set from one particular solution and a null-space basis.
Distinguish a homogeneous null subspace from a nonhomogeneous affine translate and state when the solution set contains 0.
sessions.applicationScope: Consistent exact finite systems; the affine-language distinction is geometric/structural, not projection.
sessions.transferScope: Transfer changes to model calibration: two parameter vectors produce the same target exactly when their difference is a null direction.
outOfScope: affine transformations as a separate theory
sessions.exitCondition: Given one consistent Ax=b, describe every solution and explain the role of N(A) in nonuniqueness.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. Suppose Axp=b. If n∈N(A), then A(xp+n)=Axp+An=b, so adding any null vector preserves the output. Conversely, if Ax=b too, subtracting gives A(x-xp)=0, hence x-xp∈N(A). Therefore the complete solution set is exactly xp+N(A).

This is a structural theorem, not just a solving trick. The null space describes all ambiguity left after a target b is reached. Any two solutions of the same system differ by a null vector, and any null vector moves one solution to another.

Worked example. Let A=[[1,1,0],[0,1,1]] and b=(2,1)^T. One particular solution is xp=(2,0,1). Solving Ax=0 gives N(A)=span{(-1,1,-1)}. Hence every solution is (2,0,1)+t(-1,1,-1)=(2-t,t,1-t). Direct multiplication returns b for all t.

Affine versus subspace. N(A) always contains 0. The translated set xp+N(A) contains 0 exactly when b=0: if 0 solved Ax=b, then b=A0=0. Thus a consistent nonhomogeneous solution set with b≠0 is generally not a subspace even though it is parallel to the null space.

Guided practice. For C=[[1,2,-1],[0,1,1]] and b=(3,1), find a particular solution, solve Cn=0, and write every solution as xp+t n. Then choose two different parameter values and verify their difference lies in N(C).

Distinction check. “Many solutions” does not mean arbitrary inputs work. They form one translated copy of the null space anchored at a particular solution.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. One particular solution is xp=(1,1,0). Solving Cn=0 gives n=t(3,-1,1), so every solution is (1,1,0)+t(3,-1,1). Any two choices differ by a scalar multiple of (3,-1,1), hence by a null vector.

sessions.title: Column space is the set of reachable outputs
sessions.focus: Define Col(A) as the image of the matrix map, connect consistency to membership, and extract a basis from pivot columns of the original matrix.
sessions.purpose: Turn the S05 column picture into a named output-side subspace while preventing the classic mistake of using RREF columns as if row reduction preserved literal column space.
sessions.centralCapability: Compute and interpret Col(A), select a basis from original pivot columns, and use it to decide reachability.
sessions.principalObstacle: The learner confuses Col(A) with N(A), places it in the domain, or takes pivot columns from the row-reduced matrix instead of the original matrix.
requiredOwnership: Interpret Col(A)={Ax:x∈R^n} as the range/reachable-output subspace and connect Ax=b consistency to b∈Col(A).
Use pivot positions from row reduction to choose a basis from the corresponding columns of the original matrix A.
Explain why row reduction preserves column-dependence relations/pivot indices but generally changes the literal column space, and distinguish Col(A)⊆R^m from N(A)⊆R^n.
sessions.applicationScope: Exact finite matrices; basis selection uses original columns and exact row reduction.
sessions.transferScope: Transfer presents an RREF beside the original matrix and asks the learner to audit an incorrect RREF-column basis claim.
outOfScope: row space as a developed object
sessions.exitCondition: Given A and a target, identify the correct output subspace, an original-column basis and exact reachability evidence.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. S05's column picture said Ax is a linear combination of the columns of A. The set of *all* such outputs is the column space Col(A)={Ax:x∈R^n}=span{a1,...,an}. For an m-by-n matrix, every column lies in R^m, so Col(A) is a subspace of the output space R^m. The equation Ax=b is consistent exactly when b∈Col(A).

Which original columns form a basis? Row reduction reveals pivot positions, but it changes the actual column vectors. The safe rule is: reduce A to an echelon form R, locate pivot-column indices in R, then select those indexed columns from the **original A**.

Why the index rule works. Row operations preserve the solution set of Ac=0, so a coefficient relation among A's columns exists exactly when the same coefficient vector gives a relation among R's columns. In echelon form the pivot columns are independent and every free column is a combination of earlier pivot columns. The same relation coefficients therefore hold among the corresponding original columns.

Worked example. A=[[1,2,1,3],[0,1,1,2],[1,3,2,5]] reduces to R=[[1,0,-1,-1],[0,1,1,2],[0,0,0,0]]. Pivots are in columns 1 and 2. Thus a1=(1,0,1)^T and a2=(2,1,3)^T form a basis of Col(A). Indeed a3=-a1+a2 and a4=-a1+2a2. The columns of R span a different plane in R^3; they are not the requested original-column basis.

Guided practice. For B=[[1,1,2],[1,2,3],[2,3,5]], row-reduce enough to find pivot indices, then choose a basis for Col(B) from B itself. Decide whether the third column is a new direction or a combination of the first two.

Distinction check. N(A) lives in input space and records inputs sent to zero. Col(A) lives in output space and records outputs that can be reached. Rectangular matrices make this type difference impossible to ignore.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. Column 3 equals column 1 plus column 2, while columns 1 and 2 are independent. Pivot indices are 1 and 2, so a basis for Col(B) is {(1,1,2)^T,(1,2,3)^T}; the third column adds no new direction.

sessions.title: Rank and nullity count reachable and invisible directions
sessions.focus: Define rank and nullity as dimensions of image and kernel and derive rank-nullity from pivot and free-variable counts.
sessions.purpose: Compress the structural information exposed by elimination into two basis-independent dimensions that later control injectivity, surjectivity and invertibility.
sessions.centralCapability: Compute and justify rank/nullity and use rank(A)+nullity(A)=number of input coordinates with correct dimension bounds.
sessions.principalObstacle: Rank is confused with the number of rows/columns, nullity with zero rows, or the rank-nullity sum is attached to the wrong dimension.
requiredOwnership: Define rank(A)=dim Col(A) and nullity(A)=dim N(A) and compute both from pivot/free-variable structure.
Derive rank(A)+nullity(A)=n for an m-by-n matrix from r pivot variables and n-r free variables.
Use rank≤min(m,n) and rank-nullity to audit claimed dimensions or infer missing structural information.
sessions.applicationScope: Exact finite real matrices; rank is exact algebraic rank, not tolerance-based numerical rank.
sessions.transferScope: Transfer supplies only domain/codomain sizes and a claimed nullity, requiring a consistency audit rather than row reduction.
sessions.exitCondition: Given pivot/nullspace data or matrix dimensions, infer and defend the rank-nullity structure.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. Two dimensions summarize the map's structure. The rank of A is dim Col(A): the number of independent output directions the map can reach. The nullity is dim N(A): the number of independent input directions erased by the map.

For an m-by-n matrix reduced to echelon form with r pivots, the r pivot columns of the original A form a basis of Col(A), so rank(A)=r. The n-r nonpivot variable columns give n-r free variables in Ax=0. Setting one free variable at a time to 1 produces n-r independent special solutions spanning N(A), so nullity(A)=n-r. Therefore rank(A)+nullity(A)=r+(n-r)=n, the dimension of the **domain**, not the codomain.

Worked example. Suppose a 3-by-5 matrix has RREF [[1,0,2,0,-1],[0,1,-3,0,4],[0,0,0,1,2]]. Pivots are in columns 1,2,4, so rank=3. Free variables x3,x5 give nullity=2. Their sum is 5, the input dimension. A rank cannot exceed either the number of rows or columns because Col(A)⊆R^m and no more than n columns can be independent.

Guided practice. A 4-by-6 matrix has pivot columns 1,3,4. Without solving entries, state rank, nullity, number of free variables and the largest possible rank for any 4-by-6 matrix.

Distinction check. A zero row in an echelon form can help reveal rank, but rank is not “the number of nonzero-looking rows” by definition. It is the dimension of the image; pivot count is a theorem/computational route to that dimension.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. Three pivot columns give rank 3. With six input coordinates there are 6-3=3 free variables, so nullity 3 and rank+nullity=6. Any 4-by-6 matrix has rank at most min(4,6)=4.

sessions.title: Injective and surjective mean different things for rectangular maps
sessions.focus: Connect one-to-one behavior to a trivial kernel and onto behavior to full image dimension, then separate full-column from full-row rank.
sessions.purpose: Prevent square-matrix intuition from contaminating rectangular maps and prepare the precise equal-dimension collapse used for invertibility.
sessions.centralCapability: Classify a finite linear map as injective and/or surjective from nullspace/rank evidence and translate that classification into solution behavior for Ax=b.
sessions.principalObstacle: Full rank is said without specifying row/column meaning, or injective and surjective are treated as interchangeable for every rectangular matrix.
requiredOwnership: Prove that a linear map is injective iff its null space is {0}, equivalently full column rank for an m-by-n matrix.
Characterize surjectivity onto R^m as Col(A)=R^m, equivalently rank m (full row rank).
Use matrix shape and rank to determine existence/uniqueness behavior of Ax=b and explain why a nonsquare map generally cannot be both injective and surjective.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite real coordinate maps; 'full rank' must be qualified by shape.
sessions.transferScope: Transfer describes a full-row-rank model R^4→R^2 in words and asks for preimage multiplicity without displaying entries.
sessions.exitCondition: Read shape/rank/nullity evidence as map behavior and exact-solution guarantees.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. A linear map T is injective if T(x)=T(y) forces x=y. Subtracting gives T(x-y)=0, so injectivity is exactly the statement N(T)={0}. For an m-by-n matrix, rank-nullity then gives nullity 0 iff rank=n: full **column** rank.

T is surjective onto R^m if every b∈R^m equals Ax for some x. That says Col(A)=R^m, hence rank=m: full **row** rank. These are different requirements when m≠n.

Worked contrast. A=[[1,0],[0,1],[1,1]] is 3-by-2 with two independent columns, so rank=2=n and nullity=0: it is injective R²→R³. But rank 2<3, so it is not onto R³; some targets have no solution. B=[[1,0,1],[0,1,1]] is 2-by-3 with rank 2=m, so it is onto R². Rank-nullity gives nullity 1, so it is not injective; every reachable target has multiple preimages differing by a null vector.

Guided practice. A map R³→R⁵ has rank 3. Decide injectivity and surjectivity, then state what can be guaranteed about the solution of Ax=b when a solution exists. A map R⁵→R³ also has rank 3; repeat the analysis.

Distinction check. A tall matrix can be injective without being onto; a wide matrix can be onto without being injective. Only when domain and codomain dimensions match can full column and full row rank coincide.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. For R^3→R^5 with rank 3, nullity is 0, so the map is injective but cannot be onto R^5; any existing solution is unique. For R^5→R^3 with rank 3, the map is onto but nullity is 2, so each target has infinitely many preimages.

sessions.title: For square maps, the invertibility conditions collapse together
sessions.focus: Unify injectivity, surjectivity, full rank, trivial kernel and unique solvability for square finite-dimensional linear maps before introducing an inverse algorithm or determinant.
sessions.purpose: Make invertibility a structural property of a bijective map rather than a formula available to every square matrix.
sessions.centralCapability: Determine square-map invertibility from equivalent structural evidence and prove why the conditions coincide in equal finite dimensions.
sessions.principalObstacle: Square shape is mistaken for invertibility, or inverse notation is used before one-to-one/onto structure has been established.
requiredOwnership: Define an inverse linear map as a two-sided compositional inverse and explain why invertibility requires a bijection.
For an n-by-n matrix, connect rank n, N(A)={0}, injectivity, surjectivity and unique solvability of Ax=b for every b.
Reject invertibility of a square map from a nonzero null vector or missing pivot without using determinant or eigenvalue arguments.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite real square maps; inverse existence is separated from inverse construction.
sessions.transferScope: Transfer supplies a nonzero null vector for a square matrix and asks the learner to propagate that evidence through the entire equivalence chain.
sessions.exitCondition: Given square-map structural evidence, decide whether an inverse exists and justify the decision through exact equivalences.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. An inverse of T:V→V is a map T^{-1}:V→V satisfying T^{-1}∘T=I and T∘T^{-1}=I. The first identity forces T to be injective; the second forces it to be surjective. Thus a two-sided inverse exists only for a bijection. For linear bijections, the inverse is also linear: applying T to the required additivity/scaling identities and using injectivity proves them.

For an n-by-n real matrix A, S12 and rank-nullity make several conditions equivalent. N(A)={0} iff nullity=0 iff rank=n. Rank=n equals both full column rank and full row rank because domain and codomain dimensions are both n. Thus injective iff surjective. Equivalently, every b is reachable and each has only one preimage, so Ax=b has a unique solution for every b.

Worked example. Suppose row reduction of a 3-by-3 matrix yields a pivot in every column. Then rank=3 and nullity=0, so the map is injective. Equal dimensions turn rank 3 into surjectivity as well. Hence the map is bijective and has a two-sided inverse, even before that inverse is computed.

Counterexample. A square matrix can fail completely: if Az=0 for some z≠0, then A0=Az while 0≠z, so A is not injective. Rank-nullity then gives rank<n, hence it is also not onto and no two-sided inverse exists.

Guided practice. A 4-by-4 matrix has exactly three pivots. Without determinants, state rank, nullity, injectivity, surjectivity and whether every b has a unique solution.

Distinction check. “Square” only makes the two full-rank requirements numerically comparable. It does not supply the pivots. S14 will construct an inverse only after these existence conditions are satisfied.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. Three pivots give rank 3 and nullity 1. The map is neither injective nor surjective; some b are unreachable, and any reachable b has multiple preimages. No inverse exists.

sessions.title: Construct an inverse only after it exists
sessions.focus: Derive Gauss–Jordan inverse construction from reversible row operations, verify inverses by composition, and prove inverse order reversal.
sessions.purpose: Separate inverse existence from inverse computation and make the augmented algorithm a consequence of applying the same reversible transformation to A and I.
sessions.centralCapability: Construct, verify and correctly compose exact inverse matrices while rejecting inverse notation outside its hypotheses.
sessions.principalObstacle: The learner treats [A|I] reduction as magic, solves systems by reflexively forming an inverse, or writes (AB)^{-1}=A^{-1}B^{-1}.
requiredOwnership: Construct A^{-1} by reducing [A|I] to [I|A^{-1}] and explain why the same row operations produce the inverse.
Verify a proposed inverse by two-sided multiplication and use it to solve Ax=b exactly when A is invertible.
Prove and apply (AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1} for compatible invertible square matrices, and reject inverse notation for nonsquare or singular matrices.
sessions.applicationScope: Small exact square matrices; explicit inversion is not presented as the preferred numerical method for large systems.
sessions.transferScope: Transfer changes from Gauss–Jordan construction to a composition audit with supplied inverses plus a nonsquare counterexample.
sessions.exitCondition: Compute an exact inverse when justified, verify it, and reason correctly about inverse composition order and invalid cases.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. S13 decides whether an inverse exists. If A is invertible, reversible row operations can turn A into I. Apply those *same* row operations to an attached identity matrix: [A|I]→[I|B]. If the combined row-operation map is E, then EA=I and EI=E=B, so BA=I. Because A is already known invertible, B is its unique inverse; equivalently the successful Gauss–Jordan reduction constructs A^{-1}.

Worked example. For A=[[2,1],[1,1]], start [2,1|1,0; 1,1|0,1]. Swap rows, then R2←R2-2R1, then R2←-R2, then R1←R1-R2. The result is [I|[[1,-1],[-1,2]]]. Check both AA^{-1}=I and A^{-1}A=I. For b=(5,3)^T, x=A^{-1}b=(2,1)^T.

Product inverse. If A and B are invertible, (AB)(B^{-1}A^{-1})=A(BB^{-1})A^{-1}=I and (B^{-1}A^{-1})(AB)=I. Therefore (AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}: inverse order reverses because undoing a composition reverses the stages.

Guided practice. Invert K=[[1,2],[0,1]] by [K|I], verify both products, and solve Kx=(5,2)^T. Then say why a 2-by-3 matrix cannot have a two-sided matrix inverse.

Distinction check. A^{-1} is not “1/A” and should not be formed merely because a system needs solving. This module is exact algebra; later numerical work will compare stable solver choices.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. K^{-1}=[[1,-2],[0,1]], and both KK^{-1} and K^{-1}K are I. Kx=(5,2) gives x=(1,2). A 2-by-3 map cannot be bijective between R^3 and R^2, so no two-sided square inverse exists.

sessions.title: Determinant algebra before determinant folklore
sessions.focus: Characterize the determinant structurally, derive row-operation computation rules, and separate multilinearity in one row from false whole-matrix linearity.
sessions.purpose: Give determinant calculations a principled algebraic foundation before geometric volume interpretation, singularity conclusions or cofactor-heavy recipes.
sessions.centralCapability: Compute exact determinants efficiently from structural rules and apply multiplicativity without overgeneralizing determinant as a linear function of the whole matrix.
sessions.principalObstacle: The learner memorizes cofactor formulas, assumes det(A+B)=det A+det B or det(cA)=c det A, or loses row-swap/row-scale factors during elimination.
requiredOwnership: State and use the determinant's alternating multilinear row rules with det(I)=1, distinguishing linearity in one row from linearity of the whole matrix.
Compute a square-matrix determinant by determinant-aware elimination/triangular structure while tracking row swaps and row scalings.
Use det(AB)=det(A)det(B) under its square compatible hypotheses and reject false additivity or scalar-linearity claims.
sessions.applicationScope: Exact real square matrices; cofactor expansion may appear as an optional computation, not the conceptual definition.
sessions.transferScope: Transfer is a misconception audit using I and 2I plus multiplicativity data rather than another elimination.
sessions.exitCondition: Compute and reason with determinants while stating exactly which algebraic rules are valid.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. For real n-by-n matrices, the determinant is the unique scalar function normalized by det(I)=1 that is linear in each row separately while the other rows are fixed, and alternating: swapping two rows reverses the sign. A standard finite formula guarantees existence, but the learning goal is to use the structural rules rather than memorize a large expansion.

Consequences. Multiplying one row by c multiplies the determinant by c. Replacing Ri by Ri+cRj leaves the determinant unchanged: row-linearity adds c times a determinant with two equal rows, and alternation makes that extra term zero. A row swap multiplies the determinant by -1. Therefore an upper-triangular matrix has determinant equal to the product of its diagonal entries. For [[a,b],[c,d]], these rules give ad-bc.

Worked example. For A=[[1,2,1],[2,5,3],[0,1,2]], use R2←R2-2R1 to obtain [0,1,1] and then R3←R3-R2 to obtain [0,0,1]. Row replacement did not change det, and the triangular diagonal is 1,1,1, so det(A)=1.

Whole-matrix warning. Linearity in *one row at a time* does not make det a linear map on matrices. Scaling every row of an n-by-n matrix by c gives det(cA)=c^n det(A). In general det(A+B)≠det A+det B.

Multiplicativity. For compatible square A,B, det(AB)=det(A)det(B). One structural proof fixes B and views det(AB) as an alternating multilinear function of A's rows; its value at I is det(B), so uniqueness gives det(AB)=det(A)det(B).

Guided practice. For G=[[0,1,2],[2,0,1],[0,3,1]], swap the first two rows, then use R3←R3-3R2 on the swapped matrix. Track the sign from the swap and compute det(G) from the resulting triangular matrix.

Distinction check. A determinant is one scalar invariant of a square map. It is not entrywise multiplication, not a generic linear functional on matrices, and not yet a statement about numerical stability.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. After swapping rows 1 and 2, the matrix is [[2,0,1],[0,1,2],[0,3,1]]. Replacing R3 by R3-3R2 gives diagonal 2,1,-5, whose product is -10 for the swapped matrix. One row swap changed the sign, so det(G)=10.

sessions.title: Determinant measures oriented volume collapse, not conditioning
sessions.focus: Connect det(A)=0 with noninvertibility and interpret |det A| as real volume scaling and sign as orientation.
sessions.purpose: Attach geometric and structural meaning to the determinant while sharply limiting what one scalar can establish.
sessions.centralCapability: Use determinant to diagnose singularity and exact oriented volume scaling without making unsupported numerical-sensitivity claims.
sessions.principalObstacle: Area/volume scaling is treated as the definition in every context, det=0 is remembered without structural justification, or determinant magnitude is mistaken for a condition/stability measure.
requiredOwnership: Derive and use det(A)=0 iff a real square matrix is noninvertible, connecting row-reduction/determinant rules to rank loss.
Interpret |det(A)| as the n-dimensional volume scale factor and the sign as orientation for a real square linear map.
Explain why determinant magnitude alone does not measure directional sensitivity or numerical conditioning.
sessions.applicationScope: Exact real square maps and Euclidean area/volume interpretation; no condition-number computation.
sessions.transferScope: Transfer compares two matrices with equal determinant but radically different axis scalings to expose what determinant cannot distinguish.
sessions.exitCondition: State exactly what determinant zero/nonzero and determinant magnitude/sign establish—and what they do not.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. Determinant becomes structurally decisive for square maps because row reduction links it to pivots. If elimination reaches a zero row, the triangular product is zero, so det(A)=0 and rank<n. Conversely, if every pivot exists, elimination reaches an invertible triangular matrix with nonzero diagonal; reversing the legal operations shows det(A)≠0. Combined with S13, det(A)≠0 exactly when A is invertible.

Geometry is a theorem/interpretation, not the algebraic definition used in S15. A real n-by-n linear map scales oriented n-dimensional volume by det(A). Thus |det(A)| is the ordinary volume scale factor: 2 means volumes double, 1 preserves volume magnitude, and 0 collapses n-dimensional volume into a lower-dimensional set. A negative sign reverses orientation.

Worked contrast. A=[[2,1],[1,3]] has det=5. It maps the unit square to a parallelogram of area 5 and preserves orientation; nonzero determinant also proves invertibility. C=[[1,2],[2,4]] has det=0 because its columns are dependent. The unit square collapses to a line segment, area zero, and C is not invertible.

What determinant does not say. A single product-like volume factor does not reveal how differently individual directions are stretched. Two matrices can both have determinant 1 while one stretches one axis enormously and compresses another. Numerical conditioning is a later topic and cannot be inferred from determinant size alone.

Guided practice. Compare diag(4,1/2) with diag(2,1). Compute both determinants, their area scale factors and orientation signs. Then state one directional fact that the determinant alone hides.

Distinction check. “Large determinant” is not synonymous with “stable,” and det=1 is not synonymous with “nearly identity.”
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. Both diagonal matrices have determinant 2, so both double area and preserve orientation. But the first scales the coordinate axes by 4 and 1/2 while the second scales them by 2 and 1; the determinant records only the product of those directional scales.

sessions.title: Changing coordinates does not change the vector
sessions.focus: Construct coordinate-change matrices as representations of the identity map between two ordered bases and track direction explicitly.
sessions.purpose: Prepare similarity by separating the underlying vector from its coordinate column and making basis-conversion direction a typed operation rather than a memorized P/P^{-1} formula.
sessions.centralCapability: Construct P_{B←C}, convert coordinates both ways and verify that two coordinate columns describe the same underlying vector.
sessions.principalObstacle: The change matrix is used in the wrong direction, its columns are taken from the wrong basis coordinates, or different coordinate columns are mistaken for different vectors.
entryPrerequisites: M13 ordered bases and unique coordinates
requiredOwnership: Construct P_{B←C} with columns [c_j]_B and justify [v]_B=P_{B←C}[v]_C.
Convert a vector's coordinates between two bases in both directions and verify the underlying vector is unchanged.
Use P_{C←B}=P_{B←C}^{-1} and diagnose a reversed change-of-coordinate direction.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite real vector spaces with ordered bases; no orthogonality assumption.
sessions.transferScope: Transfer begins with B-coordinates and a named C→B matrix, forcing the learner to choose the inverse rather than follow the displayed arrow blindly.
sessions.exitCondition: Given two ordered bases, convert coordinate descriptions with explicit arrow direction and preserve the underlying vector.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. A vector v does not change when we change bases; only its coordinate column changes. Let B=(b1,...,bn) and C=(c1,...,cn) be ordered bases of the same space. Define P_{B←C} to be the matrix of the identity map when the input is written in C-coordinates and the output in B-coordinates.

By S02, its jth column must be [cj]_B. If [v]_C=x, then v=Σ xj cj. Replacing each cj by its B-coordinate column gives [v]_B=P_{B←C}x. The arrow in the subscript states the direction: **C coordinates in, B coordinates out**.

Because coordinate descriptions are unique, conversion is reversible. The opposite matrix is P_{C←B}=P_{B←C}^{-1}.

Worked example. Let B be the standard basis of R² and C=(c1,c2) with c1=(1,1), c2=(1,-1). Then P_{B←C}=[[1,1],[1,-1]]. If [v]_C=(3,-1)^T, then [v]_B=(2,4)^T; directly, 3c1-c2=(2,4). The inverse (1/2)[[1,1],[1,-1]] converts (2,4) back to (3,-1).

Guided practice. Relative to basis B, let c1=2b1+b2 and c2=-b1+3b2. Build P_{B←C}. Convert [v]_C=(1,2)^T to B-coordinates, then use the inverse to recover the original C-coordinate column.

Distinction check. A coordinate-change matrix represents the identity map on vectors. It changes descriptions, not the vector itself. S18 will insert an actual operator between two such identity conversions.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. P_{B←C}=[[2,-1],[1,3]]. It sends (1,2)^T to (0,7)^T. Since P^{-1}=(1/7)[[3,1],[-1,2]], converting (0,7)^T back gives (1,2)^T.

sessions.title: Similar matrices are the same operator in different bases
sessions.focus: Derive D=P^{-1}AP by converting C-coordinates to B, applying the operator, and converting back.
sessions.purpose: Make similarity a representation theorem rather than a magic conjugation formula and establish the invariants needed before later eigenbasis work.
sessions.centralCapability: Given an operator and two bases, derive/compute its two matrix representations and justify their similarity with every coordinate direction labelled.
sessions.principalObstacle: P and P^{-1} are reversed, PAP^{-1} is written from memory, or similar matrices are treated as different operators merely because their entries differ.
requiredOwnership: Derive [T]_C=P_{B←C}^{-1}[T]_B P_{B←C} from the convert→apply→convert-back chain.
Verify on a coordinate vector that the two similar matrices produce descriptions of the same underlying operator output.
Explain that similarity preserves rank, invertibility and determinant and distinguish similarity from arbitrary left/right multiplication.

sessions.lesson:
Orient. Let A=[T]_{B←B} describe an operator T:V→V in basis B. Let P=P_{B←C}, so [v]_B=P[v]_C. To compute the output while starting and ending in C-coordinates, follow the actual pipeline:
1. convert C→B: multiply by P;
2. apply T in B-coordinates: multiply by A;
3. convert B→C: multiply by P^{-1}.
Therefore [T(v)]_C=P^{-1}AP[v]_C, so D=[T]_{C←C}=P^{-1}AP.

Worked example. Let A=[[2,0],[1,3]] and P=[[1,1],[0,1]]. Then P^{-1}=[[1,-1],[0,1]] and D=P^{-1}AP=[[1,-2],[1,4]]. For [v]_C=(2,-1), convert to B: P[v]_C=(1,-1). Apply A to get (2,-2). Convert back: P^{-1}(2,-2)=(4,-2). Directly D(2,-1)=(4,-2), confirming the same operator output in C-coordinates.

Invariants. Multiplication by an invertible P on either side does not change rank. D is invertible iff A is, because D=P^{-1}AP is a product of invertible factors exactly when A is. Determinant multiplicativity gives det D=det(P^{-1})det(A)det(P)=det(A). These properties belong to the underlying operator, not one coordinate table.

Guided practice. With A=[[1,2],[0,3]] and P=[[1,0],[1,1]], compute P^{-1}AP. Then check one C-coordinate input (1,2)^T by both the three-stage route and direct multiplication by D.

Distinction check. Similarity is not arbitrary PAQ. The left and right factors are inverse coordinate conversions tied to the same two bases. Choosing a special eigenbasis is M16, not M14.

sessions.lesson:
Orient. M14 has built several descriptions of one finite linear object. A matrix can represent a map; Ax=b asks for a preimage; N(A) records erased input directions; Col(A) records reachable outputs; rank measures the image dimension; determinant adds square-map singularity and volume information; a basis change changes coordinate tables without changing the operator.

A synthesis should therefore start from the question, not from a favorite algorithm. For reachability or ambiguity, row reduction can expose pivots and the nullspace, but a column-space basis must still come from the original matrix. For square invertibility, rank/nullspace and determinant should agree. For a new basis, derive the coordinate arrows and use similarity; do not invoke eigenvectors merely because similarity has appeared.

Worked example. Let A=[[1,1,0],[0,1,1],[1,2,1]]. The third row is the sum of the first two, so rank≤2; the first two rows/columns show rank 2. Solving Ax=0 gives N(A)=span{(-1,1,-1)} and det(A)=0, all agreeing that A is not invertible. For b=(2,1,3), xp=(1,1,0) works, so every solution is (1,1,0)+t(-1,1,-1). A basis for Col(A) can use original columns a1=(1,0,1), a2=(1,1,2), with a3=a2-a1.

If C simply swaps the first two standard basis vectors and keeps e3, its change matrix P is the corresponding permutation matrix and P^{-1}=P. The same operator in C-coordinates is P^{-1}AP=PAP; its entries change, but rank 2, determinant 0 and noninvertibility do not.

Guided practice. Reuse the worked matrix only as a *method map*: before checking, name which artifact answers each question—'Is b reachable?', 'Which inputs are invisible?', 'Which original columns form an output basis?', 'Is the square map invertible?', 'How do I rewrite it in another basis?' Do not perform new arithmetic.

Distinction check. Agreement among several valid invariants is a consistency check, not permission to substitute one definition for another. Row reduction, determinant and similarity each answer different questions.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. Reachability: solve Ax=b / test b∈Col(A). Invisible inputs: N(A). Output basis: pivot indices applied to original columns. Invertibility: square full rank/trivial kernel, equivalently nonzero determinant once S15–S16 are owned. New basis: use the identity coordinate conversion P and form P^{-1}AP.
